questions.question: A 7-billion-parameter model uses 14 GB of FP16 weights for inference and fits comfortably on a single 40 GB accelerator. Switching the same model to Adam-based training causes immediate out-of-memory failures even before activations are accounted for. Using the section's memory decomposition, which factor is most directly responsible?
choices: Adam internally re-runs the forward pass three times per step, tripling the working set of weights held in memory.

Adam adds 14 GB of FP16 gradients, 28 GB of FP32 master weights, and 56 GB of FP32 first- and second-moment estimates, pushing the standard mixed-precision training state to roughly 112 GB before activations.
Adam requires the entire training dataset to be cached in accelerator memory, which exceeds the 40 GB budget even for moderately sized corpora.
Adam disables Tensor Core execution and forces FP64 storage for every weight matrix during the backward pass.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. A standard mixed-precision Adam decomposition requires 14 GB of FP16 weights (2 bytes/param) + 14 GB of FP16 gradients (2 bytes/param) + 28 GB of FP32 master weights (4 bytes/param) + 56 GB of FP32 first- and second-moment estimates (8 bytes/param), totaling roughly 112 GB before activations. Option A is incorrect because Adam executes only one forward and backward pass per step. Option C confuses streaming input data loaded in host memory with resident accelerator state. Option D is incorrect because Adam does not force FP64 execution on Tensor Cores.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the per-step training memory footprint of an Adam-trained model from weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and identify which component dominates.

questions.question: A team's profiler shows the GPU at 18 percent utilization with periodic drops to zero, while the CPU is pinned near 100 percent on a single core and the PCIe link is mostly idle. Using the section's staged-pipeline framework, walk through how to diagnose the bubble's source and what one fix should target.
questions.answer: The signature — a single CPU core pinned near 100%, idle PCIe, and GPU utilization dropping to zero — points directly to the data loading and preprocessing stage as the binding bottleneck. In a staged pipeline, the slowest stage caps end-to-end throughput; a single-threaded Python preprocessor constrained by the GIL cannot produce batches fast enough to keep the accelerator supplied. The primary fix is to introduce process-based multiprocessing (num_workers > 0 in the DataLoader) and asynchronous prefetching, ensuring the next batch is queued in host/pinned memory before the accelerator completes its current step. Upgrading the GPU would produce zero speedup because the accelerator is completely starved by host preprocessing.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose the pipeline stage responsible for accelerator bubbles from CPU, PCIe, and GPU utilization signals, and select the optimization that addresses that specific stage.

questions.question: Four days into a large-scale mixed-precision training run on an accelerator cluster, the loss metric suddenly produces NaN across all workers, while GPU memory telemetry shows stable headroom with zero out-of-memory errors. Drawing from the chapter's discussion of training failure modes and the PaLM war story, which explanation correctly identifies the root cause and the appropriate recovery mechanism?
choices: The failure is a memory-capacity exhaustion where activations silently spilled into system RAM; the fix is to enable host memory paging.
The failure is an accelerator bubble where data prefetching stalled for more than 100 steps; the fix is to increase the DataLoader worker count.
The failure is an optimizer state desynchronization caused by Adam momentum tensors resetting to zero; the fix is to switch the optimizer to pure SGD.

The failure is a numerical-range overflow where extreme activation values exceeded FP16's maximum representable value (~6.5 × 10⁴), generating +Inf that propagated NaNs through all subsequent gradients; the fix is to restart from an uncorrupted checkpoint, skip anomalous batches, or use BF16/loss scaling.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Numerical-range overflow in FP16 occurs when activations exceed the maximum representable dynamic range (~65,504), yielding infinity (+Inf) that quickly produces NaNs throughout backpropagation. As the PaLM war story demonstrates, such numerical anomalies require rolling back to an uncorrupted checkpoint prior to the spike and skipping contaminated batches, or adopting formats with wider exponent range (such as BF16). Option A is incorrect because capacity exhaustion triggers fatal out-of-memory allocation errors rather than silent NaN propagation. Option B conflates pipeline throughput starvation (which causes GPU idleness, not arithmetic corruption) with numerical failure. Option C invents an optimizer state desynchronization mechanism that does not generate NaN loss curves.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish FP16 numerical-range overflow failures from memory-capacity exhaustion by their observable telemetry and identify operational recovery strategies.

questions.question: An engineer is told that GPU utilization on a training run sits at 30 percent and cannot rise. Under the chapter's staged-system pipeline view, which interpretation correctly identifies what an accelerator bubble represents and where to look first?
choices: A bubble is an intentional synchronization window the framework inserts to improve gradient quality; reduce the synchronization frequency.

A bubble is idle accelerator time caused by a throughput mismatch between data loading, host-to-device transfer, compute, or parameter synchronization stages; profile the four stages and locate the slowest one.
A bubble is excess on-chip cache capacity freed by activation checkpointing; tune checkpoint placement to refill it.
A bubble is an inflated arithmetic-intensity figure created by larger batch sizes; reduce batch size to bring utilization back into the compute-bound regime.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The chapter defines a bubble as silicon idleness produced when one of the four staged pipeline stages cannot keep up with the others, and prescribes profiling each stage to find the binding constraint. The 'intentional synchronization' framing mistakes a performance pathology for a feature: bubbles are something to eliminate, not insert. The 'inflated arithmetic intensity' explanation misuses the roofline vocabulary; arithmetic intensity is a property of an operation, not a pipeline-level idleness pattern. The 'cache capacity' interpretation reverses the meaning of checkpointing, which trades compute for memory and does not free cache to the user.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the systems meaning of accelerator bubbles in a staged training pipeline and the diagnostic step that follows from that meaning.

questions.question: A team running a 1.5-billion-parameter language model on a single GPU sees iteration time of 220 ms, only 25 percent GPU utilization, and memory near capacity. Storage bandwidth is 4 GB/s and the dataset is 37.3 GB of text. Using the chapter's training-systems framework, which two optimization pathways apply most directly to this signature, and which dimension of the workload (computational intensity, memory pressure, or data dependencies) does each address?
questions.answer: The 25 percent utilization indicates severe data starvation or pipeline bubbles, while near-capacity memory identifies a binding memory-pressure constraint. The first optimization pathway is asynchronous prefetching with multi-worker data loading, which overlaps batch preparation and PCIe transfer with compute, directly addressing the data dependencies and data loading stage to eliminate GPU idle bubbles. The second pathway is mixed-precision training (FP16/BF16), which halves the bytes moved per parameter and activation, addressing memory pressure to fit within accelerator capacity while enabling Tensor Core hardware to increase computational intensity. Upgrading raw compute alone would not resolve either the starved pipeline or the memory ceiling.
questions.learning_objective: Map a low-utilization training signature to the chapter's three workload dimensions and select the optimization pathways that address each.

questions.question: A 1,024-GPU training run has its prefetching pipeline well staged: PCIe is saturated overlapping with compute and gradient AllReduce is hidden behind the next forward pass. Profiling reports 38 percent MFU. Under the simplified iron law of training performance, which lever is the most actionable target for the next engineering investment, and why?
choices: Utilization η_hw — with data movement and communication already overlapped, the remaining gap to peak is composed of memory stalls, kernel-launch overhead, and synchronization slack that profiling can localize.
Peak throughput R_peak — the only way to move 38 percent MFU is to procure newer accelerators with higher advertised TFLOP/s.
Total operations O — reducing the FLOPs needed per step is the only term still movable when overlap is already achieved.
Dataset size — shrinking the dataset is the equivalent of raising η_hw because both reduce wall-clock time per epoch.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. In the Iron Law of Training Performance ($T_{\text{train}} = \frac{O}{R_{\text{peak}} \times \eta_{\text{hw}}}$), once data movement and communication are successfully overlapped behind compute, the actionable lever for systems engineering is the effective hardware utilization $\eta_{\text{hw}}$. Profiling can localize the remaining internal losses—such as memory bandwidth bottlenecks in non-GEMM layers, kernel launch latency, and small tile inefficiencies. Option B is incorrect because increasing $R_{\text{peak}}$ with newer hardware raises the theoretical ceiling without closing the 38% efficiency gap. Option C is incorrect because reducing $O$ alters the model architecture/algorithm rather than optimizing execution efficiency. Option D confuses workload reduction ($O$) with system efficiency ($\eta_{\text{hw}}$).
questions.learning_objective: Apply the simplified iron law of training performance to identify which term is the actionable engineering lever given a measured utilization and a well-overlapped pipeline.

questions.question: A team enables Tensor Cores by switching from FP32 to mixed precision, leaving the model architecture, batch size, and dataset unchanged. Under the iron law of training performance, which term is this optimization most directly targeting?
choices: Utilization η_hw, because mixed precision only removes data stalls.
Total operations O, because lower precision removes entire layers from the computational graph.
Dataset size, because mixed precision reduces the number of examples needed for convergence.
Peak throughput R_peak, because reduced-precision execution raises the accelerator's achievable FLOP/s ceiling.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Tensor Cores execute reduced-precision (FP16/BF16) matrix multiplications at a substantially higher theoretical FLOP/s ceiling than standard FP32 execution units; the chapter's iron-law mapping table explicitly assigns mixed precision to the peak throughput ($R_{\text{peak}}$) lever. Option A is incorrect because $\eta_{\text{hw}}$ measures the fraction of peak achieved, whereas mixed precision fundamentally raises the available hardware peak itself. Option B is incorrect because precision changes do not remove layers or operations from the model graph. Option C is incorrect because numerical precision format does not reduce dataset size or sample requirements.
questions.learning_objective: Classify mixed-precision training by which term of the iron law of training performance it most directly affects.

questions.question: Explain why the simplified iron law of training performance can fail to predict speedups for a small-batch debugging session even though it works well for a large-scale pretraining run on the same code.
questions.answer: The simplified Iron Law ($T_{\text{train}} = \frac{O}{R_{\text{peak}} \times \eta_{\text{hw}}}$) folds data movement and communication into the single compute term by assuming that I/O, PCIe transfers, and communication are fully overlapped behind compute. This assumption holds during large-scale pretraining where large batch sizes provide sufficient compute duration per layer to completely hide transfer and launch latencies. In a small-batch debugging session (e.g., batch size 2 or 4), the compute time per kernel collapses below the kernel launch overhead and transfer latency, breaking the overlap assumption. In this regime, execution time is dominated by serialized data transfers and launch overheads rather than pure arithmetic throughput, causing the simplified law's compute-only formula to fail.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the conditions under which the simplified form of the iron law of training performance is a valid approximation and explain the failure mode when those conditions are violated.

questions.question: An engineering manager proposes upgrading a cluster to next-generation accelerators featuring 2× the advertised peak TFLOP/s (R_peak), assuming this upgrade will automatically double the realized training utilization factor (η_hw). Under the Iron Law of Training Performance, why is this assumption flawed?
choices: Upgrading accelerators doubles total required training operations (O), perfectly canceling the peak hardware throughput improvement.
Realized utilization η_hw is mathematically fixed to 100% on any modern accelerator with Tensor Cores.

Peak throughput R_peak represents the hardware compute ceiling, whereas utilization η_hw is a pipeline property governed by memory stalls, kernel launch overhead, and data/communication bottlenecks that may remain unchanged or worsen on faster hardware.
The Iron Law of Training Performance only applies to CPU-based training systems and does not model accelerator upgrades.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Peak throughput $R_{\text{peak}}$ is a hardware specification representing theoretical compute ceiling, while $\eta_{\text{hw}}$ is the realized system efficiency ($T_{\text{train}} = \frac{O}{R_{\text{peak}} \times \eta_{\text{hw}}}$). If a workload is constrained by memory bandwidth, CPU preprocessing, or communication stalls, doubling $R_{\text{peak}}$ without addressing those pipeline bottlenecks leaves execution time largely unchanged, which actually cuts $\eta_{\text{hw}}$ in half. Option A is incorrect because total operations $O$ is a workload property independent of the accelerator hardware. Option B is incorrect because real-world workloads achieve only 30–60% MFU due to non-compute overheads. Option D is incorrect because the Iron Law is the fundamental analytical model for accelerator-based ML training.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish theoretical peak hardware throughput ($R_{\text{peak}}$) from realized system utilization ($\eta_{\text{hw}}$) in the Iron Law of Training Performance.

questions.question: Why did utilization η_hw become a more critical engineering concern by the GPT-3 era than in early CPU-era neural network training?
choices: Because training datasets became smaller, making total operations less important than utilization.
Because modern training stopped depending on matrix multiplication and became dominated by symbolic reasoning kernels.
Because training routinely ran on thousands of accelerators, so each percentage point of inefficiency translated into millions of dollars and weeks of additional wall-clock time.
Because peak throughput had become irrelevant once Tensor Cores were introduced.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. At GPT-3 scale ($O \approx 3.14 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs across thousands of GPUs), the cost of even a single percentage point of inefficiency compounds across massive accelerator fleets and months of execution, representing millions of dollars in cloud infrastructure and critical schedule delays. Option A is incorrect because pretraining datasets expanded from gigabytes to terabytes. Option B is incorrect because transformer architectures remain overwhelmingly dominated by dense matrix multiplications. Option D is incorrect because higher peak throughput from Tensor Cores makes hardware underutilization more financially punishing, not less.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why utilization becomes increasingly important as training scales to large accelerator fleets.

rationale.difficulty_progression: Hardware-mapping classification, then numerical optimizer trade-off, then activation accounting, then training-step ordering with consequence, then ridge-point application.

questions.question: Why do batched matrix-matrix operations dominate modern training accelerator design more than matrix-vector operations do, even though the underlying mathematics is similar?
choices: Because matrix-matrix operations eliminate the need to store activations for backpropagation, reducing the training memory footprint.
Because matrix-vector operations require more total memory than matrix-matrix operations for the same model, exhausting accelerator capacity faster.
Because matrix-vector operations cannot run on GPUs without CPU coordination at every step.

Because matrix-matrix operations expose much more parallel work per byte loaded — their high arithmetic intensity lets accelerators with thousands of compute units approach peak throughput, while matrix-vector workloads starve the same units on memory traffic.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMM, BLAS Level 3) achieve $\mathcal{O}(n)$ arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte transferred), enabling high data reuse in on-chip caches and keeping massive parallel ALUs compute-bound near peak throughput. Matrix-vector operations (BLAS Level 2) have an arithmetic intensity of $\mathcal{O}(1)$ FLOP/byte, making them strictly memory-bandwidth bound and leaving the vast majority of accelerator compute units idle. Option A is incorrect because activation retention is determined by backpropagation rules, not GEMM formulation. Option B is incorrect because matrix-matrix batching uses more memory per step, not less. Option C is incorrect because GPUs natively execute matrix-vector kernels.
questions.learning_objective: Identify why batched matrix-matrix operations align better with accelerator hardware than matrix-vector operations by reference to arithmetic intensity.

questions.question: A team is training a 7-billion-parameter model on accelerators with 80 GB of HBM each. Weights, gradients, and activations together occupy 64 GB per accelerator at the planned batch size. Using the section's optimizer-memory accounting, explain the systems trade-off between choosing SGD and Adam for this run.
questions.answer: Adam maintains two FP32 state vectors per parameter (first moment m_t and second moment v_t), requiring 2 × 4 bytes = 8 bytes/param. For a 7B model, Adam adds 56 GB of optimizer state alone. Adding this 56 GB to the existing 64 GB of weights, gradients, and activations yields 120 GB, which violently exceeds the 80 GB physical HBM limit and triggers an immediate OOM crash. Standard SGD (without momentum) stores zero additional state vectors (0 bytes/param), fitting comfortably within the 80 GB budget (64 GB < 80 GB). The systems trade-off is feasibility versus sample efficiency: Adam converges in fewer optimization steps but is impossible without activation checkpointing, CPU offloading, or multi-GPU sharding; SGD fits directly on a single accelerator but requires more steps and hyperparameter tuning to converge.
questions.learning_objective: Compare SGD and Adam in terms of optimizer-state memory, convergence speed, and training-system feasibility at a given memory budget.

questions.question: Why do activations often dominate the memory budget during training even when model weights already occupy several gigabytes on the accelerator?
choices: Because activations from every layer must remain resident from the forward pass until the backward pass consumes them, so total activation memory scales with depth and batch size while parameter memory is largely fixed for a given model.
Because activations are stored in FP64 even when weights are kept in FP16 or FP32, doubling their byte count.
Because activations include the raw training dataset, which grows with the number of epochs.
Because the optimizer's state vectors are accounted for as activations during the backward pass.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. During the forward pass, intermediate activation tensors at every layer must be cached in accelerator memory so the backward pass can apply the chain rule to compute gradients with respect to weights and activations. Because activation memory scales directly with batch size ($B$), sequence length ($S$), hidden dimension ($H$), and network depth ($L$), deep networks with large batches easily accumulate activations that dwarf the static parameter footprint. Option B is incorrect because activations are stored in FP16/BF16/FP32, not FP64. Option C confuses streamed input batches with retained intermediate tensors. Option D is incorrect because optimizer state is a distinct memory component tracked separately from layer activations.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why activation storage scales with depth and batch size and can exceed parameter memory during training.

questions.question: During the implementation of a custom training loop, an engineer proposes reordering the step components by executing the parameter update before completing the backward pass for all layers, or executing the backward pass before computing the loss. Why does standard backpropagation strictly enforce the causal execution sequence: (1) Forward Pass → (2) Backward Pass → (3) Optimizer Update?
choices: The optimizer update must run first to clear previous parameter values from accelerator registers before new activations can be loaded.

The forward pass generates activations required to compute loss and layer Jacobians; the backward pass uses the loss gradient and cached forward activations to compute parameter gradients via the chain rule; and the optimizer requires completed, consistent gradients to compute valid momentum and parameter updates.
The backward pass can execute independently of the forward pass, but frameworks enforce this order solely to optimize PCIe DMA transfers.
Reordering the backward pass before the forward pass is mathematically valid but disabled because it increases activation memory by 2×.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The sequence is causally and mathematically immutable: gradients are defined only with respect to a computed scalar loss from the forward pass, and backpropagation evaluates the chain rule backward from the loss using forward-cached activation tensors. The optimizer requires the fully accumulated gradients to update parameters; stepping the optimizer earlier would apply updates using missing, partial, or stale gradients from prior iterations. Option A is incorrect because parameter updates cannot occur without current gradients. Options C and D represent physical and mathematical impossibilities—the backward pass cannot compute derivatives of an uncomputed loss or without forward activations.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the causal dependency chain in a training iteration (forward pass, loss computation, backward pass, optimizer update) and why reordering breaks mathematical correctness.

questions.question: On an A100 with a ridge point near 156 FLOP/byte, a fused LayerNorm-plus-attention-softmax kernel measures roughly 5 FLOP/byte from weight and activation movement. Which optimization family is most likely to move this workload closer to the roofline, and why?
choices: Replacing the A100 with a newer accelerator advertising 2× the peak FP16 TFLOP/s.
Doubling the batch size while leaving every kernel unchanged, because larger batches always move operations across the ridge point.
Switching the optimizer from Adam to SGD while keeping every kernel unchanged.
Reducing data movement through fusion, tiling, or lower-precision weights so arithmetic intensity increases for each byte loaded into on-chip SRAM.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. With an arithmetic intensity of 5 FLOP/byte against a 156 FLOP/byte hardware ridge point, the kernel is deeply memory-bandwidth bound. To move closer to the roofline ceiling, the system must reduce global memory (HBM) traffic by fusing adjacent operations, tiling data in on-chip SRAM, or using reduced precision formats to increase the FLOPs performed per byte loaded. Option A is incorrect because a faster compute ceiling ($R_{\text{peak}}$) does not alleviate memory bandwidth starvation. Option B is incorrect because for elementwise and normalization operations, data movement scales proportionally with batch size, leaving arithmetic intensity unchanged. Option C is irrelevant to kernel-level arithmetic intensity.
questions.learning_objective: Apply arithmetic-intensity analysis and ridge-point reasoning to select the optimization family that will move a memory-bound kernel closer to the roofline.

questions.question: Which set of subsystems best describes the chapter's high-level training-system architecture, and what is the engineering value of organizing the system this way?
choices: Storage controller, compiler pass, and inference server — a layering that separates data placement from computation graph optimization.

Data pipeline, training loop, and evaluation pipeline — each subsystem has distinct resource demands (CPU/IO, accelerator compute, periodic validation), so bottlenecks can be diagnosed at the subsystem boundary instead of inside a monolithic training script.
Optimizer state manager, scheduler daemon, and checkpoint restorer — a service decomposition that mirrors how cloud training platforms expose APIs.
Tokenizer, hyperparameter tuner, and deployment gateway — a workflow decomposition centered on model-development tooling.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The pipeline architecture section organizes training as three interconnected subsystems with distinct resource profiles — ingest and preprocess on the data pipeline, forward/backward/update on the training loop, and periodic validation on the evaluation pipeline — explicitly because their interconnection points are where bottlenecks emerge. The storage-controller-and-compiler-pass grouping describes infrastructure layers, not the training architecture's stages. The optimizer-state-manager grouping lists implementation modules, not subsystems. The tokenizer-and-tuner grouping mixes a data-pipeline component with model-development tooling and ignores the runtime training loop entirely.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the major subsystems in the chapter's training pipeline architecture and justify why subsystem-level decomposition supports bottleneck diagnosis.

questions.question: A profile shows preprocessing delivering batches at 4 GB/s, host-to-device transfer at 32 GB/s, and the GPU consuming the equivalent of 12 GB/s during forward and backward passes. According to the pipeline throughput model, what determines end-to-end training throughput, and what does the answer imply for the team's next move?
choices: The average of the three rates, so the team should look for small simultaneous gains across all stages.
The transfer rate alone, because every byte must traverse PCIe before being used.
The minimum of the three rates — 4 GB/s at preprocessing — so total throughput is capped by the data pipeline, and the team should parallelize preprocessing before optimizing compute.
The GPU compute rate alone, because compute always dominates training cost.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. The pipeline throughput model the chapter introduces says end-to-end rate is bounded by the slowest stage, so the 4 GB/s preprocessor caps the system regardless of how much faster the other stages can run. Buying a faster GPU or fatter PCIe link does not help when the producer is starved — only adding preprocessing parallelism (multi-worker DataLoader, prefetching) does. Averaging the rates hides the bottleneck behavior and overstates achievable throughput. The 'compute always dominates' interpretation is the operations-manual fallacy the chapter warns about. The 'transfer dominates' answer mistakes presence on the path for being the binding stage.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the pipeline bottleneck model to determine end-to-end training throughput and select the stage to optimize first.

questions.question: Explain why CPU tokenization can become a hidden bottleneck for language-model training even on a system whose host-to-device transfer time is well under a millisecond.
questions.answer: The chapter's GPT-2 pipeline trace makes the stages comparable: a batch of 32 sequences at 1,024 tokens takes about 65.5 ms of single-threaded Python tokenization, the resulting integer-tensor transfer over PCIe takes well under a millisecond, and the forward and backward pass takes about 84.4 ms on the 32-GPU V100 cluster. Pipeline throughput is bounded by the slowest stage only when the stages overlap; run serially, the step pays both, so host preparation consumes most of the accelerator's step budget and utilization falls to roughly 56 percent. The system consequence is that adding accelerator throughput cannot recover that loss, because the lost time is spent on the CPU. The fix is multi-worker tokenization with prefetching, sized so the worker pool produces the next batch before the current step ends; the chapter's eight workers cut tokenization to about 8.2 ms and restore utilization to 95 percent.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why CPU-side preprocessing can starve GPU compute in a staged training pipeline despite low transfer latency.

questions.question: A team measures iteration time for two configurations of the same training run on the same hardware: batch size 32 yields 92 percent GPU utilization, while batch size 33 yields 71 percent utilization. What can the chapter's discussion of hardware execution granularity establish from these measurements alone?
choices: Batch size alone is insufficient to establish the cause; the team must inspect kernel launch, tensor-tile, and working-set behavior with a profiler.
Batch size 33 exceeded the L2 cache capacity, forcing every operation to spill activations to HBM.
The optimizer automatically switched to FP32 accumulation at the larger batch, halving effective compute throughput.
Larger batches always reduce gradient accuracy enough that the framework inserts extra synchronization barriers.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Warps operate on threads, and neural-network kernels generally map each sample to many threads or tiles; a batch-size change does not by itself prove that one partially filled warp caused the utilization drop. A profiler must distinguish launch-tail effects from cache, algorithm-selection, and tensor-shape changes. The optimizer and gradient-accuracy explanations invent mechanisms that frameworks do not trigger at this boundary.
questions.learning_objective: Determine when paired batch-size utilization measurements require profiling rather than attribution to wave quantization.

questions.question: A team scales an existing training run from batch size 512 to 4096 on an 8-GPU node, leaving every other hyperparameter unchanged. Per-step GPU utilization rises from 61 percent to 88 percent, but validation loss after 10,000 steps is worse than the 512-batch run at the same wall clock. What is the most likely explanation under the chapter's batch-size analysis?
choices: Each epoch now contains 8× fewer gradient updates, so the unchanged learning-rate schedule may need retuning despite higher utilization.
Larger batches changed the dtype of gradients from FP16 to FP32 automatically, slowing each step.
Larger batches removed the need for backward propagation, so the optimizer had no gradient information to update weights.
Larger batches always increase per-epoch communication volume linearly with batch size and no change in update frequency.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Total epoch work is bounded by dataset size, so an 8× larger batch means 8× fewer gradient updates per epoch. With the learning rate held constant, the optimizer takes fewer update steps per epoch; matching the baseline may therefore require retuning the learning rate and schedule. The 'gradient dtype switch' answer invents a mechanism that does not exist in the training stack. The 'backprop disappears' answer contradicts the chapter's description of larger batches as a grouping change, not a structural one. The communication claim misidentifies what scales: per-epoch communication decreases with fewer updates; per-step dense-gradient volume is roughly unchanged.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why batch-size scaling interacts with learning-rate selection to create an optimization-starved regime despite improved hardware utilization.

questions.question: Why is Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) a more informative metric than the raw accelerator-busy percentage reported by a vendor profiler when diagnosing training efficiency?
choices: Because MFU equals peak hardware throughput expressed in percent and so always sits at 100 percent on healthy hardware.
Because MFU is measured from CPU activity, so it isolates the data-loading pipeline automatically.

Because MFU counts only the FLOPs that directly advance the model toward convergence, while raw busy time also charges padding FLOPs, gradient-checkpointing recomputation, and stalled kernels that do no useful model work.
Because MFU ignores wall-clock time and therefore removes timing noise from profile traces.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. The MFU definition the chapter introduces explicitly excludes recomputation, padding, and idle-busy time from the numerator — it counts only the forward-plus-backward model FLOPs the workload needs against the accelerator's advertised peak. That is precisely why MFU diagnoses overhead that hardware-busy time hides: a kernel can be 'busy' redoing recomputation a checkpointer scheduled, and a vendor profiler will count that as utilized while MFU correctly does not. A CPU-based interpretation confuses where the metric is collected with what it measures — MFU is computed from accelerator throughput, not host activity. An MFU that 'ignores wall-clock time' contradicts the formula $T_{\text{step}} \cdot R_{\text{peak}}$ in the denominator. A 100 percent MFU is a theoretical peak, not a guaranteed healthy target.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why MFU distinguishes useful model computation from hardware-busy time and identify the overhead sources that raw utilization conflates with productive work.

questions.question: A profiler trace shows repeated white gaps where GPU activity drops nearly to zero for tens of milliseconds at a time, while CPU-side data loading shows sustained activity during those same intervals and HBM bandwidth utilization sits low. Which D·A·M class most likely dominates this trace, and how does the signature distinguish it from an adjacent class?
choices: Compute-bound — the GPU is saturated on arithmetic units; the trace would show this regardless of CPU activity.
Data-bound — the input pipeline cannot deliver batches fast enough; the discriminating signal is the GPU dropping to near zero rather than merely stalling on memory traffic.
Memory-bound — the GPU is stalled on HBM bandwidth, with the compute units idle waiting for data from device memory.
Communication-bound — inter-GPU synchronization is consuming the wall-clock budget.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The D·A·M table maps near-zero GPU utilization with active CPU input work to data-bound — the input pipeline cannot keep the accelerator fed, so it stops doing anything between batches. The discriminating signal is the GPU dropping to near zero: a memory-bound kernel still keeps the GPU's execution units active and HBM bandwidth saturated, just stalled on memory traffic rather than completely starved for input. A compute-bound interpretation contradicts the low HBM utilization the trace also shows. A communication-bound interpretation requires multi-GPU traces showing collective-operation kernels in the gaps, not idle gaps with active CPU.
questions.learning_objective: Classify a training trace as data-bound versus memory-bound by reading GPU utilization, CPU activity, and HBM bandwidth signatures together.

questions.question: A team profiles two training runs. Run A shows GPU utilization at 92 percent with HBM bandwidth saturated and CPU near idle. Run B shows GPU utilization at 18 percent with periodic drops to zero, CPU pinned, and HBM bandwidth low. Use the D·A·M taxonomy to assign each run to a bottleneck class and name the optimization family the chapter prescribes for each.
questions.answer: Run A's signature — GPU near saturation, HBM bandwidth saturated — places it on the Algorithm axis as compute-bound: the arithmetic units themselves limit throughput. The chapter prescribes algorithmic and precision-reducing fixes here — FlashAttention to lower the FLOP count of the dominant kernel, mixed precision to raise $R_{\text{peak}}$ through Tensor Cores, or simply faster hardware. Run B's signature — low GPU utilization with periodic drops to zero, pinned CPU, low HBM — is the data-bound pattern on the Data axis: the input pipeline cannot feed the accelerator. The chapter's prescription is prefetching and pipeline overlap, faster storage, and DataLoader parallelism. The system consequence is that swapping the techniques would waste effort: Run A needs algorithmic compute reduction, while Run B needs producer-side parallelism.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the D·A·M taxonomy to assign two contrasting profile signatures to bottleneck classes and select the corresponding optimization family for each.

questions.question: An engineering team observes that a training job is achieving only 22 percent MFU on an accelerator cluster. To systematically resolve this inefficiency without wasting engineering cycles on non-binding constraints, in what sequence must the team execute the chapter's diagnostic workflow?
choices: (1) Apply mixed precision and activation checkpointing → (2) Profile the optimized run → (3) Identify why throughput degraded → (4) Revert changes if MFU does not increase.
(1) Double the cluster size to dilute pipeline overhead → (2) Profile multi-node communication → (3) Optimize DataLoader worker count → (4) Tune optimizer learning rates.
(1) Rewrite custom CUDA kernels for attention → (2) Profile kernel launch occupancy → (3) Benchmark host storage throughput → (4) Validate convergence metrics.

(1) Profile the end-to-end training iteration to capture GPU, CPU, and memory traces → (2) Identify the dominant bottleneck using the D·A·M taxonomy → (3) Apply a targeted optimization to the identified constraint → (4) Re-profile the system to assess the new performance profile.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The chapter establishes the systematic workflow: Profile → Diagnose (via D·A·M) → Fix → Re-profile. Without an initial baseline profile, any optimization is guesswork that frequently targets a non-binding stage (such as optimizing GPU kernels when the pipeline is data-bound). After applying the targeted intervention, re-profiling is essential because eliminating the primary bottleneck inevitably shifts the binding constraint to another pipeline stage. Options A, B, and C represent common engineering pitfalls—applying optimizations blindly before measuring, scaling out hardware prematurely, or micro-optimizing kernels before verifying whether compute is even the bottleneck.
questions.learning_objective: Sequence and justify the systematic profile-diagnose-fix-reprofile workflow for resolving training bottlenecks.

prefetching and overlap mechanics

FlashAttention IO-aware mechanism
gradient accumulation and activation checkpointing composition
iterative re-profiling after each optimization
rationale.question_strategy: Profile-driven selection scenario, prefetching mechanism explanation, mixed-precision selective FP32, FlashAttention mechanism, memory-capacity composition, then replace the easy_tf with a scenario about a moved bottleneck after a successful optimization.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Profile interpretation, then mechanism explanation, then mechanism MCQ, then mechanism MCQ, then composition MCQ, then iterative-loop scenario.

questions.question: A profile shows 40 percent of iteration time in data loading, 35 percent in compute, and 25 percent in memory operations on a single-GPU training run. According to the section's systematic optimization framework, what should be optimized first, and why does this choice matter more than picking the most familiar technique?
choices: Gradient checkpointing, because memory is always the safest first target for memory-constrained training.
Data prefetching and pipeline overlap, because the dominant bottleneck is on the data path — optimizing compute or memory first leaves the GPU starved regardless of how fast the accelerator becomes.
Mixed precision, because compute is still a large fraction of time and Tensor Cores are the highest-leverage lever.
FlashAttention, because attention is usually the slowest kernel in transformers.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The framework prescribes profiling, identifying the dominant bottleneck, and targeting that constraint first; here data loading at 40 percent dominates. Jumping directly to mixed precision or FlashAttention optimizes a non-bottleneck and produces no speedup at the system level, because the slowest pipeline stage caps end-to-end throughput. The 'memory is always the safest first target' framing replaces evidence with habit — a memory fix on a data-bound run yields nothing. The 'attention is usually slowest' answer overgeneralizes from common transformer profiles to a workload whose own profile says otherwise.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the systematic profile-driven framework to select the optimization technique whose target matches the measured dominant bottleneck.

questions.question: Explain why prefetching can reduce iteration time from roughly the sum of fetch, preprocess, and transfer stages to roughly the maximum of those stages, and identify what condition must hold for that benefit to materialize.
questions.answer: Prefetching overlaps stages across consecutive batches: the next batch's fetch and preprocessing run on the CPU while the current batch's transfer and compute run on the accelerator. Without overlap, every iteration pays each stage's latency in series, so iteration time is the sum; with overlap, the system pays only the slowest stage's latency per iteration, so iteration time approaches the maximum. The condition for the benefit is that the pipeline buffer is deep enough and the producer stages run on hardware independent of the consumer — typically a multi-worker DataLoader on CPU plus a queue sized so the next batch is ready when the current one finishes. The system consequence is much higher accelerator utilization without changing the model itself.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how overlapping pipeline stages transforms serial latency into the maximum-stage latency and identify the buffering condition required for the transformation.

questions.question: Why does mixed-precision training keep certain quantities — such as master weights and select reductions — in FP32 even though the bulk of the forward and backward passes runs in FP16 or BF16?
choices: Because numerically sensitive accumulations and parameter updates can lose precision or underflow if held in reduced precision, while bulk matrix multiplies tolerate FP16/BF16; selective FP32 storage protects stability where it matters and exploits faster low-precision compute everywhere else.
Because FP16 and BF16 cannot run on Tensor Cores without an FP32 mirror of every activation tensor existing alongside.
Because reduced precision increases memory bandwidth demand, so FP32 is reserved for traffic-heavy paths to lower bandwidth pressure.
Because storing part of the model in FP32 is required for data parallelism but not for single-GPU training.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The mixed-precision design isolates the small subset of operations whose dynamic-range or precision requirements would otherwise destabilize training (master weight updates, certain reductions) and keeps them in FP32, while letting the large dense matrix multiplies run on Tensor Cores at FP16/BF16. The 'FP32 mirror of every activation' claim contradicts the actual implementation — only weights and select accumulators stay FP32. The 'data parallelism only' claim is mechanically wrong: mixed precision applies identically on a single GPU. The bandwidth claim inverts the direction of the actual benefit, since reduced precision halves bytes moved — keeping FP32 anywhere increases bandwidth, not decreases it.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why mixed-precision training selectively retains FP32 for numerically sensitive quantities and why that selectivity is the source of its training stability.

questions.question: What is the core systems mechanism that makes FlashAttention faster and more memory-efficient than the standard attention implementation, even though both compute the same mathematical result?
choices: It replaces softmax with ReLU so attention becomes element-wise and compute-bound.
It reduces sequence length during training so the attention matrix never exceeds cache capacity.
It stores the full S × S attention matrix in HBM once and reuses it across all backward-pass calls.
It tiles the attention computation so intermediate score and probability blocks stay in on-chip SRAM across the softmax-mask-matmul stages, never materializing the full S × S attention matrix in HBM.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. FlashAttention's mechanism is I/O-aware: it processes attention in tiles small enough to fit in on-chip SRAM, fusing softmax, masking, and matmul stages so full intermediates never spill to HBM. That eliminates $\mathcal{O}(S^2)$ intermediate storage and sharply reduces HBM traffic, which can shift attention toward the compute-bound side of the roofline. The 'shorten sequence length' claim describes a different intervention (truncation) that changes the model output and is not what FlashAttention does. The softmax-replacement claim describes a different algorithm class (linear attention). The 'store full matrix in HBM' description is the standard attention pattern FlashAttention exists to avoid.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the IO-aware tiling mechanism that lets FlashAttention reduce HBM traffic and move attention toward compute-bound execution.

questions.question: A model converges best with an effective batch size of 512, but each accelerator's memory budget admits only a micro-batch of 16 once activations and Adam optimizer state are accounted for. Which combination most directly emulates the 512 batch while also reducing activation pressure?
choices: FlashAttention plus weight decay.
Data prefetching plus operator fusion.

Gradient accumulation plus activation checkpointing — accumulation simulates the 512 batch by summing gradients over 32 micro-batches before stepping the optimizer, while checkpointing recomputes activations selectively to lower per-step activation memory.
AdamW plus cosine annealing.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Gradient accumulation lets the system emulate a larger effective batch by holding only one micro-batch's worth of activations at a time and summing gradients over multiple micro-batches before each optimizer step — the stated prescription for the 512/16 mismatch. Activation checkpointing then recomputes a chosen subset of forward activations during backprop to free their storage, addressing the activation pressure that would otherwise bind even at micro-batch 16. Prefetching plus fusion helps data starvation and memory traffic but neither emulates a larger batch nor frees activation memory. FlashAttention-plus-weight-decay mixes a kernel optimization with a regularizer; neither addresses the batch-size or activation-storage problem. AdamW-plus-cosine-annealing changes the optimizer and learning-rate schedule, neither of which affects per-step memory.
questions.learning_objective: Compose memory-capacity optimization techniques to satisfy a target effective batch size on a memory-constrained accelerator while reducing activation pressure.

questions.question: A team applies mixed precision to a transformer training run and sees compute time drop by 38 percent. They are about to declare the run optimized. Using the chapter's iterative optimization principle, explain what they should do next and what new dominant bottleneck is most plausible after a compute-side win like this.
questions.answer: The team should re-profile before declaring victory: removing one bottleneck typically reveals another, because the staged-pipeline rate is set by whichever stage is now the slowest. After mixed precision cuts compute time substantially, the data pipeline often becomes the new dominant stage — a CPU tokenizer or single-worker DataLoader that was previously masked by 200 ms of compute now appears as periodic GPU idle gaps. Memory-bandwidth-bound activation kernels can also surface as the new ceiling, since reduced precision halves bytes moved per op but does not change how many tiny activation kernels execute serially. The system consequence is that the next optimization — prefetching, multi-worker loading, or operator fusion — should be selected from a fresh profile, not from the optimization that worked last round.
questions.learning_objective: Justify why optimization is iterative by predicting which class of bottleneck most plausibly becomes dominant after a successful compute-side win.

focus_areas: data vs model parallelism trade-off under concrete memory and throughput conditions
naive model parallelism's pipeline-bubble penalty
communication tax and its effect on scaling efficiency
memory exhaustion as the binding hard limit at the 70-billion-parameter scale
single-machine-first scaling discipline
rationale.question_strategy: Replace the recall-only opener with a comparison scenario; classify naive model parallelism's failure mode; explain the communication tax; identify the binding hard limit at 70B; close with the single-node-first principle.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Scenario-based parallelism comparison, then mechanism MCQ, then SHORT analysis, then hard-limit identification, then synthesis on the scaling decision.
rationale.integration: Links the chapter's single-machine optimization toolkit to the next stage of training-system design under memory, time, and dataset-scale constraints.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Tier 1: explains both the triggers for scaling out and the major parallelism strategies used once single-machine methods are exhausted.

questions.question: A 1.5-billion-parameter model fits within a single accelerator's memory with batch size 32 and Adam optimizer state, but per-epoch wall clock is 14 hours and the team needs results in under 4 hours per epoch. They have access to 8 identical accelerators on the same node. Comparing the section's parallelism strategies, which choice is the most appropriate first step, and why does the alternative fail this scenario?
choices: Model parallelism — partition the layers across the 8 accelerators so each one holds a smaller working set; this is the right choice because layer partitioning increases per-step throughput proportionally to the number of devices.
Switch from Adam to SGD on a single accelerator to reclaim optimizer-state memory; this is the right choice because parallelism complexity should be avoided when memory is not the binding constraint.

Data parallelism — replicate the model on each accelerator and split the batch into 8 micro-batches with one AllReduce per step; this is preferred because the model already fits, so the per-step gradient synchronization is a smaller cost than the pipeline bubbles model parallelism would introduce.
Pipeline parallelism with naive layer assignment — split forward and backward passes across the 8 devices, accepting whatever bubble overhead this introduces.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Data parallelism is the natural fit when each device can hold a full model copy: it splits the batch across replicas and synchronizes gradients once per step via AllReduce, scaling throughput nearly linearly until communication becomes the bottleneck. Model parallelism is the tool for memory overflow, not throughput — layer partitioning forces sequential dependencies across devices and introduces pipeline bubbles that cost utilization. Naive pipeline parallelism makes the same mistake without microbatching. Switching to SGD addresses memory — not the binding constraint here — and gives up Adam's convergence advantage to solve a problem the team does not have.
questions.learning_objective: Choose between data parallelism and model parallelism for a memory-fits-but-too-slow training run and justify the choice by reference to which constraint the workload actually has.

questions.question: Why does naive model parallelism often deliver poor utilization even though it is the technique that lets larger models fit at all?
choices: Because each GPU must still store the full optimizer state for all partitions, exhausting memory before training begins.
Because model parallelism removes the need for batching, lowering arithmetic intensity to the memory-bound regime.
Because model parallelism requires storing the entire dataset in each node's RAM.

Because partitioning the model by layers introduces sequential dependencies, so downstream devices sit idle waiting for upstream activations to arrive — these pipeline bubbles dominate utilization until microbatched pipelining (GPipe, PipeDream) interleaves work across them.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Layer-by-layer partitioning makes device N's forward computation depend on device N-1's output, so after the first device starts, every subsequent device idles until the activations have propagated — the pipeline bubble. The chapter's footnote names microbatched pipelining (GPipe, PipeDream) as the technique that recovers most of this lost efficiency by overlapping multiple in-flight microbatches. The 'full optimizer state for all partitions' claim contradicts how model parallelism actually shards optimizer state. The 'removes the need for batching' claim invents a mechanism: minibatch execution remains essential. The 'entire dataset in each node's RAM' claim is the data-parallelism failure mode, misapplied here.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why naive model parallelism suffers from pipeline-bubble idleness and identify the technique class that recovers most of the lost efficiency.

questions.question: Explain the communication tax in distributed training and why it can erase expected speedups even when individual GPUs become more efficient. Describe one quantitative regime where the tax becomes the binding constraint.
questions.answer: Distributed training adds synchronization and gradient-exchange overhead that does not shrink in proportion to per-device compute: in ring AllReduce, each worker exchanges 2(N-1)P/N bytes for a P-byte gradient, so per-device traffic approaches 2P while per-device compute falls as devices are added. In the chapter's eight-worker, 7B-parameter example, each worker moves 1.75 × 14 GB = 24.5 GB, which takes about 1.96 s at 100 Gbps and exceeds the assumed 1 s compute time. Communication therefore becomes a larger fraction of each step, and beyond some point doubling devices stops doubling throughput. The system consequence is that scaling helps only when the workload's compute intensity is high enough relative to communication overhead — small or communication-heavy workloads see scaling efficiency collapse first.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why communication overhead limits scaling efficiency in distributed training and identify a quantitative regime where it dominates wall-clock time.

questions.question: A team plans to train a 70-billion-parameter model in FP16. Weights alone require approximately 140 GB, while the largest accelerator available to the team has 80 GB of HBM. Which hard limit identified by the section is forcing the move beyond single-device training, and what does this imply about the order in which they should explore optimizations?
choices: Memory exhaustion — the weights alone exceed single-device capacity, so single-machine optimizations cannot fit the model and the team must move to model or tensor parallelism regardless of throughput considerations.
Wall-clock time only — the team should procure a faster single accelerator before rearchitecting.
Dataset scale — the team should first attempt distributed storage tuning before considering parallelism.
Numerical precision — the team should switch to FP32 master weights to handle the larger model.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The chapter lists three hard limits that justify multi-device training: memory exhaustion, wall-clock time, and dataset scale. With 140 GB of FP16 weights against an 80 GB ceiling, the system has hit the capacity limit before considering gradients, optimizer state, or activations — single-machine optimizations like mixed precision and checkpointing reduce activations and optimizer state, but they cannot shrink weights below the precision floor. Wall-clock time may also matter, but it is not the first blocking constraint. The dataset-scale claim does not match the scenario, which describes a parameter-count problem, not an I/O problem. Switching to FP32 makes the situation worse, doubling weight memory.
questions.learning_objective: Identify memory exhaustion as the binding hard limit forcing scaling beyond a single device and explain why single-machine optimizations cannot resolve it for weight-dominated cases.

questions.question: According to the section's scaling guidance, when should a team seriously consider multi-device training?
choices: Immediately, because distributed training is usually more cost-efficient than single-node optimization.

Only after mixed precision, gradient accumulation, activation checkpointing, and data-pipeline optimization have been applied and a hard limit (memory exhaustion, wall-clock budget, or dataset scale) still remains.
Whenever the model uses Adam rather than SGD, because Adam's optimizer state always forces multi-GPU training.
As soon as GPU utilization exceeds 60 percent on a single device, because further single-node gains become difficult.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The section is explicit that teams should exhaust the single-machine optimization toolkit before accepting distributed complexity — mixed precision, accumulation, checkpointing, and pipeline optimization typically remove the binding constraint more cheaply than adding nodes. A 60 percent utilization threshold alone is not enough; the decision depends on whether one of the three hard limits persists. The 'distributed is always cheaper' framing contradicts the chapter's communication-tax analysis. The 'Adam forces multi-GPU' claim overgeneralizes: Adam's 3× optimizer state is significant but is reducible via 8-bit Adam or offloading before reaching for distribution.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate when the complexity of multi-device training is justified by reference to the single-machine optimization toolkit and the three hard limits.

focus_areas: model scaling without matched data scaling
communication overhead negating distributed speedups
hyperparameter transfer failure under batch-scale changes
pipeline neglect and the data-side blind spot
rationale.question_strategy: Replace the easy_tf with a quantitative MCQ comparing 7-billion-parameter and 20-billion-parameter models under fixed data; then communication-tax MCQ; then hyperparameter-transfer SHORT; then pipeline-neglect MCQ.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Scenario MCQ on overfitting risk, then communication-overhead MCQ, then hyperparameter SHORT, then pipeline-neglect MCQ.
rationale.integration: Synthesizes the chapter's iron-law, parallelism, and pipeline lessons into recurring failure modes.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Tier 1: consolidates high-value operational misconceptions that can waste major compute and money.

questions.question: A team has a 7-billion-parameter model performing well on a 100-million-example dataset. They scale up to a 20-billion-parameter model on the same dataset, expecting better validation performance. What does the section say about the expected validation outcome, and what does the team pay regardless?
choices: Validation performance improves linearly with parameter count, because larger models always extract more signal from a fixed dataset.
Validation performance is unchanged, because parameter count and data size are independent levers in the training equation.
Validation performance improves only if the optimizer is changed from Adam to SGD.

The validation outcome does not follow from parameter count alone; it depends on data quantity and quality, training compute, optimization, and evaluation. What does follow is the bill: roughly 3× the nonactivation training state and the compute to match.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The section's first fallacy is precisely that scale is not a monotonic lever: whether the 20-billion-parameter model outperforms the 7-billion-parameter one depends on data quantity and quality, training compute, optimization, and evaluation, and no universal accuracy penalty follows from parameter count alone. The memory arithmetic, by contrast, is certain: the larger model's nonactivation training state grows by roughly 3× under the same mixed-precision Adam recipe, and compute scales with it. The 'linear improvement' answer asserts a guarantee the section denies. The 'unchanged' answer treats capacity and data as independent levers, which they are not. The optimizer-change answer misattributes the question to optimizer choice.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why scaling parameter count against a fixed dataset guarantees a cost increase but not a validation gain.

questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates why distributed training does not automatically speed up development, even when more accelerators are added?
choices: A cluster trains faster per step, which always means faster experimentation regardless of debugging complexity.

A small communication-heavy model spends 30–50 percent of each step in gradient AllReduce, so adding more GPUs increases the synchronization fraction faster than it adds useful compute and the team observes only a 4–6× speedup on 8 GPUs instead of the expected 8×.
A large model uses BF16 instead of FP16, so data parallelism cannot be used at all and the team is forced into model parallelism.
A model uses activation checkpointing, which prevents any gradient communication from occurring across devices.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The communication-tax pitfall the section identifies plays out exactly this way: for small or communication-heavy workloads, synchronization overhead dominates and erodes the linear speedup distributed training would otherwise deliver. The BF16-blocks-data-parallelism claim is mechanically wrong: data parallelism works identically across precisions. The 'faster per step always means faster experimentation' framing ignores debugging and infrastructure complexity, which the section explicitly warns about. The activation-checkpointing-eliminates-communication claim conflates a memory-reduction technique with distributed synchronization, which still happens regardless of checkpointing.
questions.learning_objective: Identify how communication overhead can negate expected gains from distributed training and recognize the workload signature that surfaces this pitfall.

questions.question: Explain why copying hyperparameters directly from a small-batch experiment (batch 512, learning rate 0.1) to a much larger-batch training run (batch 4,096, same learning rate) can waste days of compute and end in failure.
questions.answer: Large batches change optimization dynamics: per epoch, the 4,096 batch run does 8× fewer gradient updates than the 512 batch run, so the learning rate and schedule may need retuning. The run can appear healthy for thousands of steps — loss decreases, GPU utilization is high — then fail to converge to the small-batch baseline because update frequency changed despite the lower gradient-noise floor. In the chapter's illustrative scenario, the failure surfaces days into a multi-day run, after substantial compute is spent. The system consequence is that hyperparameters need re-tuning — often starting with the linear scaling rule (η proportional to batch size) up to the critical batch size — whenever training scale changes substantially.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why hyperparameter transfer from small-batch to large-batch training can fail late in a run and identify the corrective rule the chapter prescribes.

questions.question: Which mistake does the chapter identify as especially common when teams focus only on accelerator-side optimization (kernels, mixed precision, FlashAttention) and skip end-to-end profiling?
choices: Computing LayerNorm in FP32 during mixed-precision training.
Choosing AdamW instead of SGD for a transformer.
Assuming the input pipeline is fine and only later discovering that the GPU is idle waiting for data, even though every kernel-level optimization succeeded.
Using gradient accumulation to emulate larger effective batches.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. A neglected input pipeline can leave accelerators idle, so optimizing compute kernels first risks attacking a non-bottleneck. Even a perfectly tuned attention kernel cannot help when the GPU sits waiting for the next batch. Choosing AdamW over SGD is a standard design decision the chapter neither flags as a pitfall nor ties to pipeline neglect. Gradient accumulation is a recommended technique, not a pitfall. Keeping LayerNorm in FP32 during mixed precision is the chapter's prescribed selective-FP32 stability practice.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize data-pipeline neglect as the most common operational pitfall when accelerator-side optimization succeeds without end-to-end profiling.

focus_areas: iron-law-driven optimization discipline as the chapter's central method
single-machine-first principle versus premature scaling
how utilization gains propagate through wall clock, energy, and operating cost
rationale.question_strategy: Synthesis MCQ on the chapter's main optimization approach; SHORT on the single-node-first principle; replace the easy_tf with an MCQ on how utilization improvements propagate through the iron law into runtime, energy, and cost.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Method synthesis, then single-node-first justification, then integrative reasoning about utilization's downstream consequences.
rationale.integration: Connects the iron law, profiling, and optimization composition to operating-cost and sustainability arguments.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Tier 2: integrates arguments developed earlier rather than introducing substantial new mechanisms.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the chapter's main approach to improving training performance?
choices: Use the iron law to identify whether total operations, peak throughput, or utilization is the binding lever; profile to confirm; apply targeted optimizations to that lever; then re-profile to handle the new dominant bottleneck.
Keep adding GPUs until wall-clock time is acceptable, then tune the data pipeline afterward.
Prefer optimizer changes over systems changes, because convergence dominates all hardware effects.
Reduce model size first, because system optimization rarely changes the feasible training regime.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The chapter's central discipline is profile-driven optimization guided by the iron law and the D·A·M taxonomy, with iteration after each fix. The hardware-first approach ignores the chapter's repeated warning that non-compute bottlenecks — especially memory and data flow — dominate training performance more often than compute alone. The 'optimizer-changes-dominate' framing inverts the chapter's framing of optimizer choice as a memory-versus-convergence trade-off, not a hardware-effect dominator. The 'reduce model size first' claim reverses the chapter's actual sequence, in which system optimization (mixed precision, checkpointing, accumulation) is exactly what changes the feasible training regime.
questions.learning_objective: Synthesize the chapter's profile-driven, iron-law-guided method for improving training performance.

questions.question: Why does the chapter recommend exhausting single-machine optimizations before scaling to multi-device training? Name two single-machine techniques the chapter places ahead of distribution and explain what they buy.
questions.answer: Single-machine optimizations like mixed precision, gradient checkpointing, gradient accumulation, FlashAttention, and prefetching often remove the binding constraint at far lower complexity cost than distribution: distribution adds communication overhead, debugging difficulty, and infrastructure spend that all compound failure probability. Mixed precision halves bytes moved and roughly doubles Tensor-Core throughput, raising $R_{\text{peak}}$; activation checkpointing trades roughly 33 percent additional compute for large activation-memory savings (about 70 percent in the chapter's simplified GPT-2 example), often eliminating the memory exhaustion that would otherwise force scale-out. The system consequence is that a well-optimized single node can match or beat a poorly optimized cluster while preserving faster iteration cycles — distribution should be reached for only after profiling shows a hard limit (memory, wall clock, or dataset scale) the single-node toolkit cannot resolve.
questions.learning_objective: Justify the single-machine-before-scale-out principle and connect two single-machine techniques to the iron-law levers they target.

questions.question: A team improves a 1,024-GPU training run's MFU from 30 percent to 60 percent through better pipeline overlap and a FlashAttention swap, with no change to the iron law's R_peak or the dataset. Under the chapter's framework, what is the most accurate description of how this single utilization gain propagates through the system's runtime, energy, and operating cost?
choices: Wall-clock time roughly halves, energy use drops in proportion because the run finishes faster on the same hardware drawing similar instantaneous power, and operating cost (cloud rental and electricity) drops along with energy — a single η_hw win compounds across all three downstream quantities.
Wall-clock time roughly halves, but energy use is unchanged because the accelerators draw similar power per second whether or not they are doing useful model work.
Wall-clock time, energy, and cost all stay the same, because MFU is an efficiency metric that does not affect physical resource use.
Wall-clock time stays the same, but energy and cost double because the accelerators are running 'harder.'
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Doubling $\eta_{\text{hw}}$ in the iron law's denominator roughly halves $T_{\text{train}}$ at fixed $O$ and $R_{\text{peak}}$; on the same hardware drawing similar instantaneous power, finishing in half the wall clock cuts total energy roughly in half, and cloud-rental cost (charged per accelerator-second) drops with it. The chapter's carbon-footprint perspective makes this propagation explicit: a 30 percent → 60 percent MFU improvement saves substantial kWh and tons of CO2 on a fleet-scale run. The 'energy unchanged' answer ignores that a shorter run draws power for fewer seconds. The 'no propagation' answer contradicts the iron law's structure.
